# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

# cargo_metadata - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cargo_metadata/0.23.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cargo_metadata/index.html

## Expand description

Structured access to the output of `cargo metadata` and `cargo --message-format=json`.
Usually used from within a `cargo-*` executable

See the [cargo book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/index.html) for
details on cargo itself.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Get the current crate’s metadata without default features but with all dependency information.

`let _metadata = MetadataCommand::new().exec().unwrap();`If you have a program that takes `--manifest-path` as an argument, you can forward that
to [MetadataCommand](https://docs.rs/struct.MetadataCommand.html):

```
let mut args = std::env::args().skip_while(|val| !val.starts_with("--manifest-path"));
let mut cmd = MetadataCommand::new();
let manifest_path = match args.next() {
    Some(ref p) if p == "--manifest-path" => {
        cmd.manifest_path(args.next().unwrap());
    }
    Some(p) => {
        cmd.manifest_path(p.trim_start_matches("--manifest-path="));
    }
    None => {}
};
let _metadata = cmd.exec().unwrap();
```
Pass features flags, e.g. `--all-features`.

```
let _metadata = MetadataCommand::new()
    .manifest_path("./Cargo.toml")
    .features(CargoOpt::AllFeatures)
    .exec()
    .unwrap();
```
Parse message-format output produced by other cargo commands.
It is recommended to use crates like `escargot` to produce the [Command](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html).

```
let mut command = Command::new("cargo")
    .args(&["build", "--message-format=json-render-diagnostics"])
    .stdout(Stdio::piped())
    .spawn()
    .unwrap();
let reader = std::io::BufReader::new(command.stdout.take().unwrap());
for message in cargo_metadata::Message::parse_stream(reader) {
    match message.unwrap() {
        Message::CompilerMessage(msg) => {
            println!("{:?}", msg);
        },
        Message::CompilerArtifact(artifact) => {
            println!("{:?}", artifact);
        },
        Message::BuildScriptExecuted(script) => {
            println!("{:?}", script);
        },
        Message::BuildFinished(finished) => {
            println!("{:?}", finished);
        },
        _ => () // Unknown message
    }
}
let output = command.wait().expect("Couldn't get cargo's exit status");
```

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.149/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# yew_nav_link - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew-nav-link/0.10.8/yew_nav_link/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#yew-nav-link)yew-nav-link

Navigation link component for [Yew](https://yew.rs) with automatic active
state detection.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`yew-nav-link` provides a [ NavLink](https://docs.rs/active_link/nav_link/struct.NavLink.html) component that wraps Yew Router’s

`Link` with automatic active state management. When the target route matches
the current URL, an `active` CSS class is applied.[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
[dependencies]
yew-nav-link = "0.10"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#component-syntax)Component Syntax

```
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::NavLink;
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Debug, Routable)]
enum Route {
    #[at("/")]
    Home,
    #[at("/about")]
    About
}
#[component]
fn Navigation() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::Home}>{ "Home" }</NavLink<Route>>
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::About}>{ "About" }</NavLink<Route>>
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#function-syntax)Function Syntax

For text-only links, use [ nav_link()](https://docs.rs/active_link/nav_link/fn.nav_link.html) with explicit

[mode:](https://docs.rs/active_link/mode/enum.Match.html)

`Match````
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::{Match, nav_link};
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[component]
fn Menu() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            { nav_link(Route::Home, "Home", Match::Exact) }
            { nav_link(Route::Docs, "Docs", Match::Partial) }
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#partial-matching)Partial Matching

Use `partial` prop to keep parent links active on nested routes:

```
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::NavLink;
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[component]
fn Navigation() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            // Active on /docs, /docs/api, /docs/*
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::Docs} partial=true>{ "Docs" }</NavLink<Route>>
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#css-classes)CSS Classes

| Class | Condition |
|---|---|
| `nav-link` | Always |
| `active` | Route matches |

Compatible with Bootstrap, Tailwind, and other CSS frameworks.

- Yew 0.23+
- yew-router 0.20+

# causal_replay - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/causal_replay/0.19.0/causal_replay/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#causal_replay)causal_replay

Durable backends for the [ causal](https://docs.rs/causal/0.19.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/causal/index.html) runtime, plus the cross-backend
conformance suite and replay/mirroring utilities.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-lives-here)What lives here

- **Event logs**— [- `KurrentEventLogBackend`] (feature- `kurrent`) and [- `PgEventLogBackend`] (feature- `postgres`), both implementing- `causal::EventLogBackend`.
- **Cursors & snapshots**— [- `PgReactorCheckpoint`] (projector/reactor cursors + retry counters), [- `PgSnapshotStore`] (aggregate snapshots).
- **Observability**— [- `PgReactorObserver`], [- `PgInspectorReadModel`], and [- `PgEventProjector`] (mirrors the durable log into Postgres- `causal_log`for the inspector).
- **Conformance**—- `conformance`- `EventLogBackend`impl runs the same scenario suite (append idempotency on- `event_id`, CAS via- `StreamState`, monotonic revisions, strict-after reads, isolation).
- **Replay**—- `ProjectionStream`- `PointerStore`- `REPLAY`env var.

[§](https://docs.rs#recommended-production-shape-hybrid)Recommended production shape (hybrid)

KurrentDB as the event log; Postgres for the cursor/snapshot work, which is inherently relational:

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use causal::{CheckpointStore, EngineBuilder, EventLogBackend, ReactorCheckpoint};
use causal_replay::{KurrentEventLogBackend, PgReactorCheckpoint};
let kurrent = KurrentEventLogBackend::connect("kurrentdb://localhost:2113?tls=false")?;
let pg = Arc::new(PgReactorCheckpoint::new(pool));
let engine = EngineBuilder::new(
    Arc::new(kurrent) as Arc<dyn EventLogBackend>,
    pg.clone() as Arc<dyn CheckpointStore>,
    pg as Arc<dyn ReactorCheckpoint>,
).build().await?;
```
The Postgres schema is `docs/schema.sql` in the repository; apply it
via your migration runner — backends never auto-create tables.

[§](https://docs.rs#replay-mode)Replay mode

Replay is a lifecycle state of the application, not an external tool.
The same `apply()` function runs in both live and replay mode —
[ ProjectionStream::run](https://docs.rs/stream/struct.ProjectionStream.html#method.run) checks the

`REPLAY` env var internally:```
$ server                                  # live: catch up, tail
$ REPLAY=1 server                         # replay: full read, promote, exit
$ REPLAY=1 REPLAY_TARGETS=neo4j server    # replay neo4j only
```

# causal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/causal/0.19.0/causal/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#causal)Causal

Event-sourcing runtime for Rust, [KurrentDB](https://www.kurrent.io/)-aligned:
a typed `Event → Reactor → Event` loop over an append-only event log.
Runs entirely in-memory for tests ([ MemoryStore](https://docs.rs/memory_store/struct.MemoryStore.html)); production backends
(KurrentDB event log, Postgres cursors/snapshots) live in

`causal_replay`.The vocabulary mirrors KurrentDB’s where the concepts overlap:
[ EventData](https://docs.rs/types/struct.EventData.html) /

[,](https://docs.rs/types/struct.RecordedEvent.html)

`RecordedEvent``causation_id` /
`workflow_id`, [(0-indexed),](https://docs.rs/types/struct.StreamRevision.html)

`StreamRevision`[for optimistic concurrency,](https://docs.rs/types/enum.StreamState.html)

`StreamState``{category}-{subject_id}` stream names.[§](https://docs.rs#guarantees)Guarantees

- **At-least-once delivery, idempotent appends**— reactor outputs carry deterministic- `event_id`s, so crash-redelivery dedups on append.
- **Replay determinism**— no wall-clock inside consumer bodies; aggregate state is a pure fold of the log.
- **Quiescence**—- `emit(...).settled()`resolves when the event’s workflow chain has been observed by every consumer.
- **OCC where you opt in**— the- `Engine::append`decider path enforces- `StreamState`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use causal::{Ctx, EngineBuilder, Event, Events, Reactor};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use uuid::Uuid;
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct OrderPlaced { order_id: Uuid, total: f64 }
impl Event for OrderPlaced {
    const NAME: &'static str = "order_placed";
    fn subject_id(&self) -> Uuid { self.order_id }
}
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct ShipmentRequested { order_id: Uuid }
impl Event for ShipmentRequested {
    const NAME: &'static str = "shipment_requested";
    fn subject_id(&self) -> Uuid { self.order_id }
}
struct ShipOnPlaced;
#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl Reactor for ShipOnPlaced {
    type Trigger = OrderPlaced;
    const NAME: &'static str = "ship_on_placed";
    async fn react(&self, t: &OrderPlaced, _ctx: Ctx<'_>) -> anyhow::Result<Events> {
        Ok(causal::events![ShipmentRequested { order_id: t.order_id }])
    }
}
let engine = EngineBuilder::memory()
    .with_reactor(ShipOnPlaced)
    .build()
    .await?;
// Persists the event, stamps causation/workflow, and resolves once
// ShipOnPlaced has reacted and its output has landed in the log.
engine.emit(OrderPlaced { order_id: Uuid::new_v4(), total: 99.99 })
    .settled()
    .await?;
```
The `#[event]` macro (feature `macros`, on by default) generates the
[ Event](https://docs.rs/event/trait.Event.html) impl from a struct declaration
(

`#[event(name = "order_placed", subject_id = "order_id")]`); the
example hand-rolls it to show the full trait surface.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use event::`- [event_type_for](https://docs.rs/event/fn.event_type_for.html);
- `pub use event::`- [stream_name_for](https://docs.rs/event/fn.stream_name_for.html);
- `pub use event::`- [Event](https://docs.rs/event/trait.Event.html);
- `pub use aggregate::`- [Aggregate](https://docs.rs/aggregate/trait.Aggregate.html);
- `pub use aggregate::`- [Apply](https://docs.rs/aggregate/trait.Apply.html);
- `pub use aggregator::`- [Aggregator](https://docs.rs/aggregator/struct.Aggregator.html);
- `pub use projector::`- [Projector](https://docs.rs/projector/trait.Projector.html);
- `pub use multi_projector::`- [MultiProjector](https://docs.rs/multi_projector/trait.MultiProjector.html);
- `pub use reactor::`- [Events](https://docs.rs/reactor/struct.Events.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [aggregate](https://docs.rs/aggregate/index.html)
- `Aggregate`marker +- `Apply<F: Event>`extension.
- [aggregator](https://docs.rs/aggregator/index.html)
- Aggregator registry — manages aggregate definitions and state.
- [checkpoint_](https://docs.rs/checkpoint_store/index.html)- store
- Per-consumer cursor storage + reactor retry-tracking traits.
- [clock](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html)
- Calendar-clock injection — one half of Primitive 6’s two-clock rule.
- [consumer_](https://docs.rs/consumer_lease/index.html)- lease
- Exclusive consumer lease — prevents two servers from processing the same consumer’s triggers simultaneously.
- [contexts](https://docs.rs/contexts/index.html)
- Single `Ctx`type passed to all consumer bodies. Three separate context types would add no safety beyond what the runtime already enforces.
- [decision_](https://docs.rs/decision_store/index.html)- store
- `DecisionStore`— one durable decision per- `(consumer, trigger)`.
- [effect_](https://docs.rs/effect_store/index.html)- store
- `EffectStore`— make side-effecting reactors safe under at-least-once delivery.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- `Engine`+- `EngineBuilder`— the public runtime surface.
- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- `Event`trait — application-facing surface for events.
- [event_](https://docs.rs/event_id_registry/index.html)- id_ - registry
- `EventIdRegistry`— an authoritative, unbounded global index of appended- `event_id`s, so- `Any`(idempotent) appends can recognize a redelivery no matter how deep the original output is buried.
- [event_](https://docs.rs/event_log/index.html)- log
- Append-only event log trait — the write side of the durable event store.
- [event_](https://docs.rs/event_type/index.html)- type
- Single owner of event-kind validation and matching.
- [failure](https://docs.rs/failure/index.html)
- The retry taxonomy (BLOCKING-2) — error classes, declared by the reactor, that decide retry policy. No blanket policy in either direction: blanket bounded-retry turns a ten-minute infra outage into a mass manual-replay incident; blanket infinite-retry turns a poison payload into a permanently wedged partition.
- [memory_](https://docs.rs/memory_store/index.html)- store
- In-memory backend: `EventLogBackend`+`CheckpointStore`+`ReactorCheckpoint`+`SnapshotStore`(+`ReactorObserver`and the inspector read surface).
- [multi_](https://docs.rs/multi_projector/index.html)- projector
- `MultiProjector`— declared-subscription cross-domain event consumer.
- [projection](https://docs.rs/projection/index.html)
- Projection / consumer start-position configuration.
- [projection_](https://docs.rs/projection_failure/index.html)- failure
- Poison-park failure handling shared by the serial projection runners
(`ProjectionRunner``MultiProjectorRunner`
- [projection_](https://docs.rs/projection_runner/index.html)- runner
- Runner that drives `Projector``EventLogBackend::read_all`.
- [projector](https://docs.rs/projector/index.html)
- `Projector`trait — idempotent at-least-once external state.
- [reactor](https://docs.rs/reactor/index.html)
- `Reactor`trait — pure decisions producing new facts.
- [reactor_](https://docs.rs/reactor_observer/index.html)- observer
- `ReactorObserver`— telemetry hook for reactor execution and aggregate folds. The engine calls these methods at well-defined points so observability sinks (the in-memory inspector backend, external tracing, etc.) can capture causal-chain history without the engine itself having to know about durability of trace data.
- [reactor_](https://docs.rs/reactor_runner/index.html)- runner
- Partitioned runner for `Reactor`
- [snapshot_](https://docs.rs/snapshot_store/index.html)- store
- Snapshot persistence trait — separate from the event log so the snapshot backend can be swapped independently (Postgres log + S3 snapshots, Kurrent log + Postgres snapshots, etc.). Backends implement this trait directly.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)
- Core data types for the causal event log.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [events](https://docs.rs/macro.events.html)
- Universal return macro for `Reactor::react``Events`

- [async_](https://docs.rs/attr.async_trait.html)- trait
- [event](https://docs.rs/attr.event.html)
- Marks a struct as a causal fact, generating its `causal::Event`impl.
- [projectors](https://docs.rs/attr.projectors.html)
- Turns a module of plain async functions into registered

- [reactors](https://docs.rs/attr.reactors.html)
- Turns a module of plain async functions into registered [`Reactor`]s — the fn body is the Primitive-2 body, untouched; the macro removes trait ceremony only.

# causal_inspector_utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/causal_inspector_utils/0.19.0/causal_inspector_utils/

## Expand description

Describe DSL for the causal inspector UI.

Provides [ Block](https://docs.rs/enum.Block.html) — a set of visual primitives that handlers return to
describe their current state. Blocks are serialized to JSON in the store
and rendered inline on reactor nodes in the causal flow diagram.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use causal_inspector_utils::{Block, ChecklistItem, State};
let blocks = vec![
    Block::progress("Scrape phases", 0.75),
    Block::checklist("Steps", vec![
        ChecklistItem::new("Fetch data", true),
        ChecklistItem::new("Transform", false),
    ]),
    Block::status("Pipeline", State::Running),
];
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Checklist](https://docs.rs/struct.ChecklistItem.html)- Item
- A checklist item with text and done state.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Block](https://docs.rs/enum.Block.html)
- A visual primitive rendered inline on reactor nodes in the causal flow diagram.
- [State](https://docs.rs/enum.State.html)
- Named state for a `Block::Status`

# hrdr_app - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hrdr-app/0.2.1/hrdr_app/

## Expand description

`hrdr-app` — the UI-agnostic application core shared by hrdr’s frontends.

Logic that is identical regardless of how it’s rendered lives here so the TUI
(`hrdr-tui`) and GUI (`hrdr-gui`) share one implementation instead of each
reimplementing it. Today: the slash-command registry, alias resolution, and
“quit command” detection. More (help metadata is already here) will move in
as the frontends converge.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [expand_](https://docs.rs/expand_msg/index.html)- msg
- `/expand`status lines (both frontends show the same wording).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/struct.ChatPalette.html)- Palette
- hrdr’s chat-role colors as resolved from an hjkl theme (before frontend fallbacks).
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigWatcherGuard.html)- Watcher - Guard
- Keeps a config watch alive; drop it to stop watching.
- [CtxGauge](https://docs.rs/struct.CtxGauge.html)
- The context gauge’s raw data, for frontends that can draw a real progress bar (the GUI) instead of the character-cell fill the text runs encode.
- [Find](https://docs.rs/struct.FindState.html)- State
- The `/find`/`/next`/`/prev`state machine: active query + last-visited message number. Both frontends hold one (the GUI behind signals) and route the returned`FindAction`
- [Highlight](https://docs.rs/struct.HighlightCache.html)- Cache
- Incremental code-block highlighter with a small LRU of in-progress blocks.
- [History](https://docs.rs/struct.HistoryBrowser.html)- Browser
- Input-history browsing shared by the frontends: record with
consecutive-duplicate skip + `MAX_HISTORY`
- [Resume](https://docs.rs/struct.ResumePlan.html)- Plan
- What restoring a session changes beyond the host’s own state swap: the working directory to adopt (if any) and the system lines to show, in order.
- [Role](https://docs.rs/struct.RoleStyle.html)- Style
- Renderer-agnostic style spec: which theme slots to paint with. `fg: None`means inverted text (black) over`bg`— used by the context-gauge fill.
- [Save](https://docs.rs/struct.SaveOutcome.html)- Outcome
- The result of an auto-save: the session’s file id, and whether this call was the one that first assigned it (so the frontend can notify once).
- [Status](https://docs.rs/struct.StatusInputs.html)- Inputs
- Everything the status bar shows, gathered by the frontend.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/struct.StatusRun.html)- Run
- One styled run of text within a status section.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/struct.StatusSeg.html)- Seg
- One status-bar section: a drop `priority`(higher = dropped first when the TUI truncates) and its styled runs.`gauge`carries the context gauge’s raw data when this section is it — text frontends use the pre-split fill/rest runs, pixel frontends draw a real bar from the gauge.
- [UiConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.UiConfig.html)
- Frontend/display configuration. Loaded from the same
`~/.config/hrdr/config.toml`+`HRDR_*`env vars as`hrdr_agent::AgentConfig`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [CtxLevel](https://docs.rs/enum.CtxLevel.html)
- How full the context window is, for the gauge’s fill color.
- [Diff](https://docs.rs/enum.DiffLineKind.html)- Line - Kind
- Semantic role of one unified-diff line, for `/diff`coloring — the classification both frontends map onto their theme.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/enum.Entry.html)
- One rendered item in the transcript.
- [Expand](https://docs.rs/enum.ExpandMode.html)- Mode
- What `/expand`should do to tool output (parsed by the shared dispatcher; applied by the frontend, which owns the expansion state).
- [Find](https://docs.rs/enum.FindAction.html)- Action
- What a `/find`,`/next`,`/prev`, or`/goto`resolved to. The frontends only differ in how they scroll — the parsing, cycling, wrap-around, and status lines are all here.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/enum.LineKind.html)- Kind
- How an async result line should be displayed.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.StatusBarMode.html)- BarMode
- How the status bar behaves when it doesn’t fit the terminal width.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.StatusRole.html)- Role
- Semantic color role of a status run — frontends map these to theme colors.
- [Theme](https://docs.rs/enum.ThemeSlot.html)- Slot
- Theme slot a semantic role colors from. Both frontends’ themes expose these eight colors (under their own field names); mapping slot → concrete color is the only per-frontend piece.
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/enum.TimestampStyle.html)- Style
- Per-message timestamp display style.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [BELL_](https://docs.rs/constant.BELL_MIN_SECS.html)- MIN_ - SECS
- Minimum turn duration before the finish nudge fires (terminal bell in the TUI, desktop notification in the GUI) — quick replies stay silent.
- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_TODO_TTL.html)- TODO_ - TTL
- Default lifetime (in turns) a completed TODO item stays visible before it’s pruned: the turn it finishes plus four more.
- [HELP_](https://docs.rs/constant.HELP_GROUPS.html)- GROUPS
- Commands grouped by theme, for a readable help listing.
- [INIT_](https://docs.rs/constant.INIT_PROMPT.html)- PROMPT
- Instruction sent to the model by `/init`to author an`AGENTS.md`.
- [INPUT_](https://docs.rs/constant.INPUT_MAX_ROWS.html)- MAX_ - ROWS
- Max text rows the input box auto-grows to (both frontends).
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_HISTORY.html)- HISTORY
- Max input-history entries kept (in memory and on disk).
- [PROJECT_](https://docs.rs/constant.PROJECT_DOCS_LOADED_MSG.html)- DOCS_ - LOADED_ - MSG
- Startup notice when `AGENTS.md`was gathered into the system prompt.
- [RELOAD_](https://docs.rs/constant.RELOAD_HOT_MSG.html)- HOT_ - MSG
- [RELOAD_](https://docs.rs/constant.RELOAD_MANUAL_MSG.html)- MANUAL_ - MSG
- `/reload`+ hot-reload status lines (both frontends).
- [RESUME_](https://docs.rs/constant.RESUME_BUSY_MSG.html)- BUSY_ - MSG
- Guard shown when `/resume`is attempted mid-turn (the running turn holds the agent mutex: the message swap would silently no-op while the transcript and session id switched, and the turn’s autosave would then overwrite the resumed session’s file with the old conversation).
- [SLASH_](https://docs.rs/constant.SLASH_COMMANDS.html)- COMMANDS
- The slash commands, as `(name, one-line description)`. Frontends render this however they like (a completion popup, a`/`menu, a help screen).
- [TOOL_](https://docs.rs/constant.TOOL_ARGS_PREVIEW.html)- ARGS_ - PREVIEW
- Character width of the one-line tool-args preview (both frontends).
- [TUI_](https://docs.rs/constant.TUI_ONLY_COMMANDS.html)- ONLY_ - COMMANDS
- Commands only the TUI implements today (terminal-coupled, or not yet ported
to the GUI). Canonical names; aliases resolve before matching. The GUI
filters these out of completion and `/help`, and answers with a notice instead of sending the text to the model.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.CommandHost.html)- Host
- The capabilities a frontend exposes so the shared commands can drive it.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [active_](https://docs.rs/fn.active_file_token.html)- file_ - token
- If an `@…`file mention is being typed at the end of`input`, return the byte offset of the`@`and the partial query after it. Requires the`@`to start a token (preceded by start-of-input or whitespace) with no whitespace after it.
- [age_](https://docs.rs/fn.age_completed_todos.html)- completed_ - todos
- Age out finished TODO items in place. Stamps each completed item with the
`turn`it was first seen finished (in`stamps`, keyed by content), then drops any completed item that has been finished for`ttl`turns. Stamps for items no longer present as completed are forgotten, so a re-completed item ages from scratch. Pending / in-progress items are kept.
- [agent_](https://docs.rs/fn.agent_cwd.html)- cwd
- The tools’ working directory: the agent’s cwd when the lock is free (a turn may hold it), else the process cwd.
- [cancel_](https://docs.rs/fn.cancel_message.html)- message
- The cancel notice both frontends show (with the discarded-queue count).
- [classify_](https://docs.rs/fn.classify_diff_line.html)- diff_ - line
- Classify one line of a unified diff (see `DiffLineKind`
- [clipboard_](https://docs.rs/fn.clipboard_copy_status.html)- copy_ - status
- Copy `text`to the OS clipboard, returning the status line both frontends show.`cb`is the frontend’s long-lived clipboard handle (`None`when the platform has none).
- [clipboard_](https://docs.rs/fn.clipboard_read_text.html)- read_ - text
- Read the OS clipboard as text (`/paste`).
- [compaction_](https://docs.rs/fn.compaction_message.html)- message
- The system line a finished compaction shows — identical in both frontends.
- [config_](https://docs.rs/fn.config_mtime.html)- mtime
- Modified-time of the user config file, for hot-reload dedup guards.
- [conversation_](https://docs.rs/fn.conversation_to_json.html)- to_ - json
- The conversation’s user/assistant turns as a JSON array of `{n, role, content}`.
- [conversation_](https://docs.rs/fn.conversation_to_markdown.html)- to_ - markdown
- The conversation’s user/assistant turns as Markdown.
- [ctx_](https://docs.rs/fn.ctx_level_slot.html)- level_ - slot
- The gauge-fill color slot for a context-usage level (also used by the GUI’s real progress-bar gauge).
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_kind_slot.html)- kind_ - slot
- Diff-line coloring semantics (additions green, deletions red, hunk headers
in the user accent, file headers/context dim) — shared with
`crate::classify_diff_line`
- [dispatch](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch.html)
- Handle a `/…`command shared by both frontends. Returns`true`if it was a recognized command (and thus shouldn’t be sent to the model). Unknown input returns`false`so the caller can pass it to the model or handle it locally.
- [display_](https://docs.rs/fn.display_dir.html)- dir
- Display form of `cwd`, with the home directory collapsed to`~`.
- [endpoint_](https://docs.rs/fn.endpoint_health_warning.html)- health_ - warning
- Probe the endpoint (list its models) and return a warning line when it
looks unreachable or doesn’t advertise `model`;`None`when healthy. The startup health-check core — both frontends spawn it and surface the warning as a system line before the first turn.
- [expand_](https://docs.rs/fn.expand_mentions.html)- mentions
- Expand `@file`mentions in`input`by appending the referenced files’ contents (resolved under`cwd`), for sending to the model. Each distinct readable`@path`is attached once under a trailing “Referenced files” section, truncated at 100 KiB on a char boundary; unreadable/missing/ duplicate references are skipped. Returns`input`unchanged when nothing resolves. The display copy should keep the bare`@path`; only the sent copy carries the expansion.
- [export_](https://docs.rs/fn.export_conversation.html)- conversation
- Write the conversation to a file per a `/export [--json] [file]`argument, returning the path written and its line count. With no file, a timestamped`hrdr-transcript-<date>.{md,json}`in`cwd`is used.
- [find_](https://docs.rs/fn.find_hits.html)- hits
- 1-based message numbers whose user/assistant text contains `query`(case-insensitive substring). Message numbers count only user/assistant entries, matching the numbering the frontends display.
- [first_](https://docs.rs/fn.first_message_since.html)- message_ - since
- The number of the first user/assistant message stamped at/after `cutoff`.`times`is parallel to`entries`(index i is entry i’s local timestamp).
- [fmt_](https://docs.rs/fn.fmt_count.html)- count
- Compact token count: `840`,`12.4k`,`1.8M`.
- [git_](https://docs.rs/fn.git_branch.html)- branch
- Current git branch (or short detached-HEAD sha) by walking up from `cwd`to the repo root and reading`.git/HEAD`. Cheap, no subprocess.
- [git_](https://docs.rs/fn.git_working_diff.html)- working_ - diff
- The working-tree `git diff`for`cwd`(stdout on success, stderr message on failure). Shared by`/diff`.
- [goto_](https://docs.rs/fn.goto_action.html)- action
- `/goto <N | 5m | 1h | top | end>`— resolve- `arg`against a transcript with- `count`displayed messages.- `first_since(cutoff)`returns the number of the first message at/after that instant (the frontend’s timestamp lookup).
- [help_](https://docs.rs/fn.help_body.html)- body
- The grouped, aligned `/help`body: a`Commands`header followed by each`HELP_GROUPS`section with its commands and descriptions. Frontends append their own keybinding “Tips:” tail (those keys differ per frontend).
- [help_](https://docs.rs/fn.help_body_for.html)- body_ - for
- Like `help_body``show`accepts — so a frontend’s`/help`advertises exactly what it supports (the GUI passes its`CommandHost::supports_command`
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_known_command.html)- known_ - command
- Whether `cmd`(with or without the leading`/`; aliases welcome) is a registered slash command at all — used by frontends to tell “command I don’t support” apart from “not a command, send it to the model”.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_quit_command.html)- quit_ - command
- Whether a submitted line is a common “quit the session” command, matched
across popular CLIs/REPLs/editors so users feel at home: bare `exit`/`quit`, the`/exit``/quit``/bye`slash family, and vim’s`:q`family.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_tui_only.html)- tui_ - only
- Whether `cmd`(with or without the leading`/`; aliases welcome) is a TUI-only command per`TUI_ONLY_COMMANDS`
- [last_](https://docs.rs/fn.last_fenced_block.html)- fenced_ - block
- The last fenced (`…`) code block in markdown`md`, without the fences.
- [latest_](https://docs.rs/fn.latest_session_for_cwd.html)- session_ - for_ - cwd
- The most recent saved session for `cwd`that has actual conversation content (more than just the system prompt) — the startup auto-resume lookup shared by both frontends.`None`= nothing to resume, start fresh.
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_history.html)- history
- Load persisted single-line input history (most recent `MAX_HISTORY`
- [load_](https://docs.rs/fn.load_hjkl_theme.html)- hjkl_ - theme
- Load an hjkl theme TOML from `path`, falling back to hjkl’s bundled default when`path`is`None`or fails to parse (both frontends’ load policy).
- [message_](https://docs.rs/fn.message_count.html)- count
- Number of user/assistant messages in the transcript.
- [messages_](https://docs.rs/fn.messages_to_entries.html)- to_ - entries
- Rebuild display entries from a restored message history (`/resume`, startup auto-resume) — shared so the TUI and GUI reconstruct identically. User and non-empty assistant texts become entries; each assistant`tool_calls`entry is paired with its`role:"tool"`result by call id (the`Error:`prefix convention marks a failed call). Other roles are skipped. Frontends map the returned entries into their own representation (the TUI stores them as-is, the GUI wraps each in its reactive signals).
- [nth_](https://docs.rs/fn.nth_message_text.html)- message_ - text
- The text of the Nth (1-based) user/assistant message, if any.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_system_handler.html)- system_ - handler
- Launch the OS default handler for `path`(`xdg-open`on Linux/BSD,`open`on macOS,`start`on Windows), detached — the child outlives the call.
- [panel_](https://docs.rs/fn.panel_bg_rgb.html)- bg_ - rgb
- Panel background RGB for code blocks and tool output: the syntect theme’s background with a dark fallback. Frontends convert to their color type.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_duration.html)- duration
- Parse a relative duration like `30s`,`5m`,`1h`,`2d`into seconds.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_msg_range.html)- msg_ - range
- Parse a message spec: `N`→`(N, N)`, or`N-M`→`(N, M)`(1-based, inclusive). Returns`None`for invalid or zero/reversed ranges.
- [persist_](https://docs.rs/fn.persist_history.html)- history
- Persist input history (one entry per line; multi-line entries are skipped to keep the line-based file well-formed). Best-effort — filesystem errors are silently ignored.
- [rank_](https://docs.rs/fn.rank_file_matches.html)- file_ - matches
- Rank file paths against an `@file``query`and return the best (up to 8). Empty query keeps input order (shortest paths first); otherwise basename prefix-matches rank above anywhere-substring matches, ties broken by shorter path then lexicographically. Case-insensitive.
- [relative_](https://docs.rs/fn.relative_time.html)- time
- Human-friendly elapsed time since `then`, with compound units for the larger ranges (`now`,`42s ago`,`5m ago`,`1h30m ago`,`2d3h ago`).
- [reload_](https://docs.rs/fn.reload_invalid_message.html)- invalid_ - message
- Invalid config file on reload: keep the current settings and warn.
- [reload_](https://docs.rs/fn.reload_project_docs.html)- project_ - docs
- Re-read `AGENTS.md`into the system prompt (used by`/reload`and after an`/init`turn writes the file). Returns the standard system line when project docs were loaded,`None`when there are none.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_alias.html)- alias
- Resolve a slash-command alias to its canonical name (case-insensitive), so users coming from other agents can use familiar names. Unknown names pass through unchanged.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_under.html)- under
- Resolve `path`against`base`: absolute paths pass through unchanged, relative ones are joined onto`base`.
- [resume_](https://docs.rs/fn.resume_plan.html)- plan
- The shared `/resume`semantics both frontends apply: follow the session’s working directory (in-process only) and surface the same notices.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_compaction.html)- compaction
- The shared compaction core (`/compact`and threshold auto-compaction): lock the agent and summarize.`Ok((before, after))`with`before == after`means there was nothing to compact.
- [save_](https://docs.rs/fn.save_agent_session.html)- agent_ - session
- Async wrapper over `save_session``CommandHost::autosave`); the TUI’s synchronous`try_lock`autosave keeps its own snapshot but funnels into the same`save_session`
- [save_](https://docs.rs/fn.save_session.html)- session
- Persist a conversation as a session (best-effort; filesystem errors are
swallowed). Returns `None`when there’s nothing worth saving yet (no user message). Otherwise it builds and writes the session under`cwd`, assigning a stable file id from the name when`existing_id`is`None`(via`hrdr_agent::unique_session_id``label`overrides the auto-derived name (the first user line); pass`None`to use the derived one.
- [session_](https://docs.rs/fn.session_list_text.html)- list_ - text
- The `/sessions`listing as a display string. With`all`, every directory’s sessions are shown (each row tagged with its cwd); otherwise only those whose cwd matches`cwd`. Returns a friendly empty-state message when there are none.
- [session_](https://docs.rs/fn.session_name_from.html)- name_ - from
- A short session name derived from the first user message (first line, trimmed,
capped at 60 chars). Falls back to `"untitled"`when there’s no usable text.
- [session_](https://docs.rs/fn.session_saved_notice.html)- saved_ - notice
- The one-time notice when a session file is first created.
- [sessions_](https://docs.rs/fn.sessions_all_flag.html)- all_ - flag
- Whether a `/sessions`argument requests every directory’s sessions.
- [should_](https://docs.rs/fn.should_auto_compact.html)- auto_ - compact
- Whether the context usage warrants a proactive compaction before more work
— the `auto_compact`threshold check, shared by both frontends.`last_prompt_tokens`is the latest model call’s prompt size.
- [should_](https://docs.rs/fn.should_bell.html)- bell
- Whether a finished turn warrants the nudge: the knob is on and the turn ran
at least `BELL_MIN_SECS`
- [slash_](https://docs.rs/fn.slash_completions.html)- completions
- Commands matching the in-progress `/…`input (empty once a space is typed).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_file_index.html)- file_ - index
- Build the `@file`completion index off the UI thread —`walk_files``on_done`receives the file list there (send it back through your UI channel).
- [startup_](https://docs.rs/fn.startup_config_warning.html)- config_ - warning
- Startup warning when the config file exists but is invalid (the running config already fell back to defaults + env).
- [status_](https://docs.rs/fn.status_role_style.html)- role_ - style
- The one place the status-bar color semantics live — frontends resolve the returned slots against their theme instead of re-deciding role → color.
- [status_](https://docs.rs/fn.status_sections.html)- sections
- Build the status sections in display order. Priorities (drop order under truncation, highest first): ttft 6, effort 5, tokens 4, branch 3, model 2, context 1, dir 0.
- [syntax_](https://docs.rs/fn.syntax_set.html)- set
- The bundled syntax set, deserialized once.
- [syntect_](https://docs.rs/fn.syntect_theme.html)- theme
- The highlight theme (base16-ocean.dark, falling back to any bundled theme).
- [transcript_](https://docs.rs/fn.transcript_to_json.html)- to_ - json
- The conversation as a pretty-printed JSON array of `{n, role, time, content}`objects (user/assistant messages only).`times`is parallel to`entries`.
- [transcript_](https://docs.rs/fn.transcript_to_text.html)- to_ - text
- The transcript as Markdown-ish text (user/assistant/system/diff/tool lines;
reasoning and stats are omitted). Used by `/copy all`and`/export`.
- [turn_](https://docs.rs/fn.turn_stats_line.html)- stats_ - line
- The per-turn stats line both frontends append after a completed turn
(`✓ N tok · tok/s · elapsed · ttft · ctx`).`None`when the turn produced nothing measurable.`ttft_secs`is time-to-first-token; the token rate is measured from the first token, not the request start.
- [walk_](https://docs.rs/fn.walk_files.html)- files
- Collect relative file paths under `root`for`@file`completion. In a git repo, honors`.gitignore`/`.ignore`(and parents/global) +`.git/info/exclude`via the`ignore`crate; outside one, falls back to a manual walk that skips known VCS/build and hidden directories.
- [walk_](https://docs.rs/fn.walk_files_gitignore.html)- files_ - gitignore
- Gitignore-aware walk (ripgrep’s walker).
- [watch_](https://docs.rs/fn.watch_config.html)- config
- Watch the user config file, invoking `on_change`(from a background thread/task) on every modification — the unified hot-reload source for both frontends. Uses an OS-level watcher (inotify/FSEvents/…) on the config’s parent directory (so atomic saves via rename are caught) and falls back to 2s mtime polling when a watcher can’t be created. The callback should just ping the frontend’s channel; dedup (e.g. ignoring self-inflicted writes from persisting a setting) is the receiver’s job.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [HlLine](https://docs.rs/type.HlLine.html)
- One highlighted line: `(style, text)`runs. Text keeps syntect’s trailing newline (frontends trim as their renderer needs).
- [Line](https://docs.rs/type.LineFuture.html)- Future
- A future producing a system line to display (empty = show nothing). The host spawns it on its runtime and pipes the result to its transcript.
- [Rgb](https://docs.rs/type.Rgb.html)
- An RGB triple resolved from a theme.

](https://coveralls.io/github/baoyachi/shadow-rs)`shadow-rs` allows you to access properties of the build process and environment at runtime, including:

- `Cargo.toml`information, such as the project version
- Dependency information
- Git information, such as the commit that produced the build artifact
- What version of the Rust toolchain was used in compilation
- The build variant, e.g. `debug`or`release`
- ... And more!

Strongly recommend using **shadow-rs** on the [LSP](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/) service developed in Rust.

You can use this crate to programmatically check where a binary came from and how it was built.

# BuildPattern

The BuildPattern enum defines strategies for triggering package rebuilding. **Default mode is  Lazy**.

- `Lazy`: The lazy mode. In this mode, if the current Rust environment is set to- `debug`, the rebuild package will not run every time the build script is triggered. If the environment is set to- `release`, it behaves the same as the- `RealTime`mode.
- `RealTime`: The real-time mode. It will always trigger rebuilding a package upon any change, regardless of whether the Rust environment is set to- `debug`or- `release`.
- `Custom`: The custom build mode, an enhanced version of- `RealTime`mode, allowing for user-defined conditions to trigger rebuilding a package.

# Setup

### 1) Modify `Cargo.toml` fields

Modify your `Cargo.toml` like so:

```
[]
 = "build.rs"
[]
 = {  = "{latest version}",  = false }
[]
 = "{latest version}"
```
About

`build = "build.rs"`,this is an optional addition where, by default, build points to the build.rs file. It is recommended to use it as such. However, if your build script file is not named build.rs, please manually specify it. For example:`build = "gen.rs"`.

use shadow;
shadow!;
```
The `shadow!` macro uses the given identifier to create a module with that name.

## Setup for `no_std`

Add this to your Cargo.toml

```
[]
 = {  = "{latest version}",  = false }
[]

```
#### Reproducibility

This tool includes the current time in the binary which would normally make it non-reproducible.
However, it respects the [ SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH variable](https://reproducible-builds.org/docs/source-date-epoch/) - if
set to a Unix timestamp it will override the value of build time.

# shadow_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/shadow-rs/2.0.0/target-redirect/shadow_rs/

## Expand description

`shadow-rs`: Build-time information stored in your Rust project (binary, lib, cdylib, dylib).

`shadow-rs` allows you to access properties of the build process and environment at runtime, including:

- `Cargo.toml`information, such as the project version
- Dependency information
- Git information, such as the commit that produced the build artifact
- What version of the Rust toolchain was used in compilation
- The build variant, e.g. `debug`or`release`
- … And more!

You can use this crate to programmatically check where a binary came from and how it was built.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

- Check out the [example_shadow](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow)for a simple demonstration of how`shadow-rs`might be used to provide build-time information at run-time.
- Check out the [example_shadow_hook](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow_hook)for a demonstration of how custom hooks can be used to add extra information to`shadow-rs`’s output.
- Check out the `builtin_fn`example`shadow-rs`provides.

[§](https://docs.rs#setup)Setup

[§](https://docs.rs#1-modify-cargotoml-fields)1) Modify `Cargo.toml` fields

Modify your `Cargo.toml` like so:

```
[package]
build = "build.rs"
[dependencies]
shadow-rs = { version = "{latest version}", default-features = false }
[build-dependencies]
shadow-rs = "{latest version}"
```
Optional Dependencies:

- `git2`- *(enabled by default)*— Use- `libgit2`as a backend for git operations

[§](https://docs.rs#2-create-buildrs-file)2) Create `build.rs` file

Now in the root of your project (same directory as `Cargo.toml`) add a file `build.rs`:

[§](https://docs.rs#3-integrate-shadow)3) Integrate Shadow

In your main Rust file (usually `main.rs` or `lib.rs`), add this:

The `shadow!` macro uses the given identifier to create a module with that name.

[§](https://docs.rs#4-use-shadow-constants)4) Use Shadow Constants

You can now use the module defined with `shadow!` to access build-time information.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main(){
    println!("debug:{}", shadow_rs::is_debug()); // check if this is a debug build. e.g 'true/false'
    println!("branch:{}", shadow_rs::branch()); // get current project branch. e.g 'master/develop'
    println!("tag:{}", shadow_rs::tag()); // get current project tag. e.g 'v1.3.5'
    println!("git_clean:{}", shadow_rs::git_clean()); // get current project clean. e.g 'true/false'
    println!("git_status_file:{}", shadow_rs::git_status_file()); // get current project statue file. e.g '  * examples/builtin_fn.rs (dirty)'
    println!("{}", build::VERSION); //print version const
    println!("{}", build::CLAP_LONG_VERSION); //print CLAP_LONG_VERSION const
    println!("{}", build::BRANCH); //master
    println!("{}", build::SHORT_COMMIT);//8405e28e
    println!("{}", build::COMMIT_HASH);//8405e28e64080a09525a6cf1b07c22fcaf71a5c5
    println!("{}", build::COMMIT_DATE);//2021-08-04 12:34:03 +00:00
    println!("{}", build::COMMIT_AUTHOR);//baoyachi
    println!("{}", build::COMMIT_EMAIL);//xxx@gmail.com
    println!("{}", build::BUILD_OS);//macos-x86_64
    println!("{}", build::RUST_VERSION);//rustc 1.45.0 (5c1f21c3b 2020-07-13)
    println!("{}", build::RUST_CHANNEL);//stable-x86_64-apple-darwin (default)
    println!("{}", build::CARGO_VERSION);//cargo 1.45.0 (744bd1fbb 2020-06-15)
    println!("{}", build::PKG_VERSION);//0.3.13
    println!("{}", build::CARGO_TREE); //like command:cargo tree
    println!("{}", build::CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR); // /User/baoyachi/shadow-rs/ |
    println!("{}", build::PROJECT_NAME);//shadow-rs
    println!("{}", build::BUILD_TIME);//2020-08-16 14:50:25
    println!("{}", build::BUILD_RUST_CHANNEL);//debug
    println!("{}", build::GIT_CLEAN);//false
    println!("{}", build::GIT_STATUS_FILE);//* src/lib.rs (dirty)
}
```

# shadow_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shadow-rs/2.0.0/shadow_rs/index.html

## Expand description

`shadow-rs`: Build-time information stored in your Rust project (binary, lib, cdylib, dylib).

`shadow-rs` allows you to access properties of the build process and environment at runtime, including:

- `Cargo.toml`information, such as the project version
- Dependency information
- Git information, such as the commit that produced the build artifact
- What version of the Rust toolchain was used in compilation
- The build variant, e.g. `debug`or`release`
- … And more!

You can use this crate to programmatically check where a binary came from and how it was built.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

- Check out the [example_shadow](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow)for a simple demonstration of how`shadow-rs`might be used to provide build-time information at run-time.
- Check out the [example_shadow_hook](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow_hook)for a demonstration of how custom hooks can be used to add extra information to`shadow-rs`’s output.
- Check out the `builtin_fn`example`shadow-rs`provides.

[§](https://docs.rs#setup)Setup

[§](https://docs.rs#1-modify-cargotoml-fields)1) Modify `Cargo.toml` fields

Modify your `Cargo.toml` like so:

```
[package]
build = "build.rs"
[dependencies]
shadow-rs = { version = "{latest version}", default-features = false }
[build-dependencies]
shadow-rs = "{latest version}"
```
Optional Dependencies:

- `git2`- *(enabled by default)*— Use- `libgit2`as a backend for git operations

[§](https://docs.rs#2-create-buildrs-file)2) Create `build.rs` file

Now in the root of your project (same directory as `Cargo.toml`) add a file `build.rs`:

[§](https://docs.rs#3-integrate-shadow)3) Integrate Shadow

In your main Rust file (usually `main.rs` or `lib.rs`), add this:

The `shadow!` macro uses the given identifier to create a module with that name.

[§](https://docs.rs#4-use-shadow-constants)4) Use Shadow Constants

You can now use the module defined with `shadow!` to access build-time information.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

    println!("git_status_file:{}", shadow_rs::git_status_file()); // get current project statue file. e.g '  * examples/builtin_fn.rs (dirty)'
    println!("{}", build::VERSION); //print version const

    println!("{}", build::RUST_CHANNEL);//stable-x86_64-apple-darwin (default)
    println!("{}", build::CARGO_VERSION);//cargo 1.45.0 (744bd1fbb 2020-06-15)

- Re-exported from the const_format crate

- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_replace.html)- replace
- Re-exported from the const_format crate

- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_splice.html)- splice
- Re-exported from the const_format crate

- Re-exported from the const_format crate
Alternative version of `str_splice`
- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split.html)- split
- Re-exported from the const_format crate

- [str_](https://docs.rs/macro.str_split_pat.html)- split_ - pat
- Re-exported from the const_format crate
Version of `str_split``&'static [&'static str]`.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/shadow-rs/2.0.0/src/shadow_rs/lib.rs.html

# shadow_rs/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![doc(html_logo_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/master/shadow-rs.png")]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! `shadow-rs`: Build-time information stored in your Rust project (binary, lib, cdylib, dylib).
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! `shadow-rs` allows you to access properties of the build process and environment at runtime, including:
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! * `Cargo.toml` information, such as the project version
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! * Dependency information
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! * Git information, such as the commit that produced the build artifact
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! * What version of the Rust toolchain was used in compilation
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! * The build variant, e.g. `debug` or `release`
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! * ... And more!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! You can use this crate to programmatically check where a binary came from and how it was built.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! # Examples
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! * Check out the [example_shadow](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow) for a simple demonstration of how `shadow-rs` might be used to provide build-time information at run-time.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! * Check out the [example_shadow_hook](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/example_shadow_hook) for a demonstration of how custom hooks can be used to add extra information to `shadow-rs`'s output.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! * Check out the [`builtin_fn` example](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/tree/master/examples/builtin_fn.rs) for a simple demonstration of the built-in functions that `shadow-rs` provides.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! # Setup
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! ### 1) Modify `Cargo.toml` fields
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! Modify your `Cargo.toml` like so:
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! ```toml
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! [package]
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! build = "build.rs"
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! [dependencies]
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! shadow-rs = { version = "{latest version}", default-features = false }
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! [build-dependencies]
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! shadow-rs = "{latest version}"
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```
[35](https://docs.rs#35)#![cfg_attr(feature = "document-features", doc = document_features::document_features!())]
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! ### 2) Create `build.rs` file
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! Now in the root of your project (same directory as `Cargo.toml`) add a file `build.rs`:
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! ```ignore
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! fn main() {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     ShadowBuilder::builder()
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         .build_pattern(BuildPattern::RealTime)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!         .build().unwrap();
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ```
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ### 3) Integrate Shadow
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! In your main Rust file (usually `main.rs` or `lib.rs`), add this:
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ```ignore
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! use shadow_rs::shadow;
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! shadow!(build);
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ```
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! The `shadow!` macro uses the given identifier to create a module with that name.
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! ### 4) Use Shadow Constants
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! You can now use the module defined with `shadow!` to access build-time information.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```ignore
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! fn main(){
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!     println!("debug:{}", shadow_rs::is_debug()); // check if this is a debug build. e.g 'true/false'
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     println!("branch:{}", shadow_rs::branch()); // get current project branch. e.g 'master/develop'
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!     println!("tag:{}", shadow_rs::tag()); // get current project tag. e.g 'v1.3.5'
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     println!("git_clean:{}", shadow_rs::git_clean()); // get current project clean. e.g 'true/false'
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     println!("git_status_file:{}", shadow_rs::git_status_file()); // get current project statue file. e.g '  * examples/builtin_fn.rs (dirty)'
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!     println!("{}", build::VERSION); //print version const
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!     println!("{}", build::CLAP_LONG_VERSION); //print CLAP_LONG_VERSION const
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     println!("{}", build::BRANCH); //master
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!     println!("{}", build::SHORT_COMMIT);//8405e28e
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     println!("{}", build::COMMIT_HASH);//8405e28e64080a09525a6cf1b07c22fcaf71a5c5
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     println!("{}", build::COMMIT_DATE);//2021-08-04 12:34:03 +00:00
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     println!("{}", build::COMMIT_AUTHOR);//baoyachi
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     println!("{}", build::COMMIT_EMAIL);//xxx@gmail.com
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     println!("{}", build::BUILD_OS);//macos-x86_64
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     println!("{}", build::RUST_VERSION);//rustc 1.45.0 (5c1f21c3b 2020-07-13)
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!     println!("{}", build::RUST_CHANNEL);//stable-x86_64-apple-darwin (default)
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     println!("{}", build::CARGO_VERSION);//cargo 1.45.0 (744bd1fbb 2020-06-15)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     println!("{}", build::PKG_VERSION);//0.3.13
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!     println!("{}", build::CARGO_TREE); //like command:cargo tree
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     println!("{}", build::CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR); // /User/baoyachi/shadow-rs/ |
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!     println!("{}", build::PROJECT_NAME);//shadow-rs
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     println!("{}", build::BUILD_TIME);//2020-08-16 14:50:25
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     println!("{}", build::BUILD_RUST_CHANNEL);//debug
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     println!("{}", build::GIT_CLEAN);//false
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     println!("{}", build::GIT_STATUS_FILE);//* src/lib.rs (dirty)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! }
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! ```
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! ## Clap
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! You can also use `shadow-rs` to provide information to command-line interface crates such as [`clap`](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/). An example of this can be found in [`example_shadow`](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/blob/master/example_shadow/src/main.rs).
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! For the user guide and further documentation, see the [README of `shadow-rs`](https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs).
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # List of Generated Output Constants
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! All constants produced by `shadow-rs` are documented in the module created with [`shadow!`], so `rustdoc` and your IDE will pick it up.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! ```
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! pub const PKG_VERSION: &str = "1.3.8-beta3";
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! pub const PKG_VERSION_MAJOR: &str = "1";
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! pub const PKG_VERSION_MINOR: &str = "3";
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! pub const PKG_VERSION_PATCH: &str = "8";
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! pub const PKG_VERSION_PRE: &str = "beta3";
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! pub const RUST_VERSION: &str = "rustc 1.45.0 (5c1f21c3b 2020-07-13)";
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! pub const BUILD_RUST_CHANNEL: &str = "debug";
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! pub const COMMIT_AUTHOR: &str = "baoyachi";
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! pub const BUILD_TIME: &str = "2020-08-16 13:48:52";
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! pub const BUILD_TIME_2822: &str = "Thu, 24 Jun 2021 21:44:14 +0800";
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! pub const BUILD_TIME_3339: &str = "2021-06-24T15:53:55+08:00";
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! pub const BUILD_TIMESTAMP: i64 = 1624548839;
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! pub const COMMIT_DATE: &str = "2021-08-04 12:34:03 +00:00";

## Expand description

Add a module with the provided name which contains the build information generated by `shadow-rs`.

[§](#example)Example

[ⓘ](#)```
use shadow_rs::shadow;
shadow!(my_build_information);
fn main() {
    println!("I'm version {}!", my_build_information::VERSION);
}
```

The convention, however, is to use `shadow!(build);`.
